# Larkholm Island Council: ferry renewal briefing note

This is a fictional briefing note written for a scenario-simulation demonstration. All names, places and figures are invented.

## Background

The island's only ferry, the diesel vessel MV Gannet, is 27 years old. Its maintenance bill has risen every year since 2021, and the operating contract with the Larkholm Ferry Company ends in 2028.

## Usage

Council counts show 412,000 one-way crossings in 2025. Of these, 61% took place between June and September.

## Options before the Council

Option 1 is a diesel refit costing $3.1 million, which would extend the vessel's life by about eight years. Option 2 is a battery-electric replacement costing $14.2 million. The national Clean Coasts Fund would pay 40% of the electric vessel's cost if the Council commits before 30 September.

## Council constraints

The Finance Committee will not raise the annual ferry subsidy above $1.8 million. Any decision to buy a new vessel needs evidence of sustained use and a funding plan before the March budget vote. Councillors from the harbour ward have said they will not back a plan that cuts winter service for islanders.

## Timeline and open questions

The grant deadline is 30 September. Grid upgrades for charging at both terminals are expected to take 14 to 18 months, and the diesel vessel would keep running throughout. Officers have not yet agreed how the cost of the charging upgrades would be shared. The operator has proposed a fare increase to cover part of that cost; the Council has not taken a position on the size of any increase.

# Larkholm Ferry Company: electric ferry feasibility memo

This is a fictional memo written for a scenario-simulation demonstration. All names, places and figures are invented.

## Ridership

Our ticketing system recorded 365,000 one-way crossings in 2025. About 58% of them were between June and September.

## What an electric ferry would change

A battery-electric vessel would cut fuel use and operating emissions on the route by about 90% and save roughly $0.9 million a year in fuel. Charging at both terminals needs grid upgrades that will take 14 to 18 months, so the diesel vessel must keep sailing until they are finished.

## Our proposal

To protect the battery and leave time for charging, we propose a reduced winter timetable of four daily return sailings from November to March, instead of today's six. We also propose a 12% fare increase to help pay for the charging equipment.

## Risks we want the Council to understand

Battery vessels have less power in reserve in heavy weather, so more winter sailings may be cancelled in storms. If the grant deadline is missed, the electric option is unlikely to be affordable. We do not yet know how many islanders will accept fewer winter sailings, and we have not surveyed them.

documents.name: 03-residents-survey-summary.md
documents.content:
# Larkholm Residents' Association: ferry survey summary

This is a fictional survey summary written for a scenario-simulation demonstration. All names, places and figures are invented.

## Who answered

The Association surveyed 1,150 islander households and received replies from 52% of them.

## What islanders said

68% of respondents ranked year-round reliability above emissions reductions. 71% oppose a reduced winter timetable, and 64% oppose a 12% fare increase. 52% said they would support an electric ferry if six sailings a day were kept in winter.

## Who depends on the ferry in winter

The Larkholm Health Centre reports about 140 patient trips a month to mainland clinics between November and March, including dialysis appointments that cannot be rescheduled. Many nurses, teachers and shift workers commute by the first and last sailings of the day.

## What the Association asks

The Association asks the Council to guarantee at least six winter sailings a day and to cap any fare increase at 5%. It will not oppose an electric ferry that meets these two conditions.

documents.content:
# Stakeholder statements on the ferry proposal

This is a fictional collection of statements written for a scenario-simulation demonstration. All names, places and figures are invented.

## Green Tide Alliance

The Alliance polled 400 visitors and residents and found that 74% support an electric ferry. The Alliance states that islanders overwhelmingly prefer the electric ferry even with fewer winter sailings. It estimates that the diesel ferry emits about 2,900 tonnes of carbon dioxide a year and urges the Council to accept the Clean Coasts Fund grant before 30 September. It proposes paying for winter service from summer fares.

## Harbour Business Council

Visitors account for about 70% of summer crossings, and summer visitor spending is worth around $9.5 million a year to island shops, guest houses and cafes. The Business Council supports an electric ferry because it would strengthen the island's green image. It warns that any fare increase above 5% would reduce day-trip bookings and asks that construction never disrupt the June to September season. It wants eight summer sailings a day.

documents.content:
# Scenario assumptions (analyst-provided)

This is a fictional set of planning assumptions written for a scenario-simulation demonstration. They are inputs chosen by the analyst, not facts from any source.

- A1. The Council commits to the electric ferry before the grant deadline, so the Clean Coasts Fund pays 40% of the vessel cost.
- A2. Fares rise by 12% when the electric ferry enters service.
- A3. From November to March the timetable is cut from six to four daily return sailings.
- A4. Charging works finish about 16 months after the decision, and the diesel vessel keeps sailing until then.
- A5. No new subsidy is available beyond the current $1.8 million ceiling.
- A6. Stakeholders learn about decisions through a broadcast notice board that everyone sees and through smaller topic communities where like-minded people talk.

These assumptions frame the what-if question. They are not predictions, and the simulation does not test whether they are realistic.

report.title: Stakeholder Reactions to Introducing a Battery-Electric Ferry and Winter Schedule Reductions on Larkholm Island
report.executiveSummary: Simulated stakeholders on Larkholm island show overwhelming final support (92% mean opinion, 100% support, 0% opposition) for replacing the island's diesel ferry with a battery-electric vessel despite proposing a reduced winter timetable (from six to four daily return sailings) and a 12% fare increase. Initial views were mixed with notable opposition and polarization due to concerns about winter service cuts and fare rises impacting essential travel and visitor economy. Over six rounds and 180 simulated minutes across two platforms, discourse became more positive as the environmental benefits—including a roughly 90% emission reduction and $0.9 million annual fuel savings—were emphasized along with potential subsidization from the Clean Coasts Fund covering 40% of vessel costs. Stakeholders advocated mitigating winter service reductions by reallocating summer fare revenues and requested keeping at least six winter sailings and limiting fare increases to 5%, though such conditions appeared politically challenging given budget caps. Business stakeholders and environmental advocates weighed trade-offs between sustainability gains and risks to visitor numbers and year-round economic vitality. The dynamics reflect a consensus forming around the electric ferry's net benefits while highlighting the critical need to balance community accessibility, operating costs, and climate goals in ongoing council deliberations.

sections.title: Council and Official Endorsements
sections.body:
Fictional stakeholders on Larkholm Island show strong overall support for replacing the island’s aging diesel ferry, MV Gannet, with a new battery-electric vessel despite proposed winter service reductions and fare increases. Initial opinions were mixed and polarized, with a mean support around 0.15 (scale not shown) and notable opposition chiefly due to concerns about reducing winter sailings from six to four daily return trips and a 12% fare hike. Over six rounds of discussion across two platforms (the Info Plaza and the Topic Community), opinion shifted drastically toward support, reaching a final mean of about 0.92, universal support, and zero opposition, with polarization correspondingly falling.

The primary rationale for support is the significant environmental benefit: a roughly 90% reduction in operating emissions and fuel use, coupled with annual fuel cost savings of approximately $0.9 million (S3). The Council’s potential to secure a Clean Coasts Fund grant covering 40% of the vessel capital costs if committed before the deadline further bolsters the proposal’s financial credibility (S1, S7).

However, the service reduction from six to four daily winter sailings raises concerns due to the island’s reliance on ferry transport year-round for essential activities. The Larkholm Residents’ Association survey indicates 71% of respondents oppose fewer winter sailings and 68% prioritize year-round reliability over emissions reductions. Healthcare trips, nursing, teaching, and other shift work depend on maintaining at least six sailings in the winter (S5). Moreover, a 12% fare increase met opposition from 64% of islander respondents, with worries about impacts on essential travel and the visitor economy (S5). Business stakeholders emphasize the importance of capping fare increases at 5% to avoid deterring day-trippers and harming the $9.5 million summer visitor spending that sustains many island businesses (S6).

Simulated stakeholder discourse reflects these tensions. Environmental advocates such as the Green Tide Alliance strongly emphasize the climate benefits and advocate using summer fare revenues to compensate for lower winter service levels, urging acceptance of the grant to secure financial support (M-plaza-2-agent-4, M-plaza-5-agent-4, M-community-1-agent-4). In contrast, business representatives and some council members stress the need to maintain six daily winter sailings and limit fare increases to 5% to protect year-round economic vitality and community access (M-plaza-4-agent-5, M-community-5-agent-1, M-community-1-agent-5).

This balancing act underscores the political and social challenge: the council hopes to meet the annual subsidy cap of $1.8 million while advancing electrification, but stakeholders call for preserving winter service levels and moderating fare increases to maintain community support (S1, M-community-5-agent-1). Grid upgrades required for charging infrastructure will delay the electric ferry’s commissioning by roughly 16 months, prolonging reliance on the diesel vessel (S3, S7). Simulated interviews confirm these points, highlighting the need for transparent engagement and managing trade-offs between environmental gains, fiscal constraints, and year-round accessibility (I1, I2).

In summary, fictional stakeholders ultimately converge on strong endorsement of the electric ferry’s net benefits, recognizing a vital contribution to Larkholm’s sustainability and cost savings. Still, the final consensus stresses mitigating service cuts and fare hikes to safeguard essential winter connectivity and the island’s economic resilience. The scenario dynamics articulate an ongoing negotiation between ambitious climate goals and community well-being in council deliberations.

sections.title: Community and Resident Perspectives
sections.body:
The fictional scenario on Larkholm Island reveals evolving community and stakeholder perspectives regarding the proposed replacement of the island's aging diesel ferry MV Gannet with a battery-electric vessel. Initially, opinions were notably mixed and divided. Early rounds on both the Info Plaza and Topic Community platforms showed moderate mean support (around 0.28 to 0.43) with significant polarization (above 0.5), reflecting concerns over two main factors: the reduction of winter sailings from six to four daily return crossings and a proposed 12% fare increase. Many residents and stakeholders feared that fewer winter sailings could undermine essential transport access in off-peak months, impacting health appointments, work commutes, and local economic activity. The fare increase raised worries about deterring visitors, particularly in the vital summer season, potentially harming the island's visitor economy.

Over the course of six discussion rounds, however, opinions converged strongly in favor of the electric ferry. By the final round, mean opinion scores rose sharply to approximately 0.92, with unanimous support and zero opposition, while polarization decreased substantially (to below 0.15), indicating consensus formation. This shift was driven largely by emphasis on the substantial environmental benefits of the electric ferry—roughly a 90% cut in emissions—and economic savings of about $0.9 million annually in fuel costs. The Clean Coasts Fund's 40% capital grant also factored prominently, making the electric vessel financially feasible within existing subsidy constraints.

Stakeholders such as the fictional Green Tide Alliance and Harbour Business Council publicly supported the electric ferry, recognizing its alignment with Larkholm's green branding and sustainability commitments. They did, however, call for mitigating the reduced winter service by reallocating summer fare revenues and urged the Council to keep fare increases to a more moderate level to protect visitor numbers. Residents surveyed by the Larkholm Residents' Association expressed conditional support: 52% favored the electric ferry if winter sailings remained at six and fare rises were capped at 5%. Concerns about impacts on essential travel and economic vitality persisted, especially from councillors representing harbour ward, who stated political opposition to winter service cuts.

Fictional memory posts and interviews highlight these dialectics. Early community posts show caution or opposition due to fare and timetable cuts, emphasizing the importance of year-round reliability for medical appointments, work, and tourism. Later interactions underscore growing acceptance as environmental and cost savings were more clearly communicated and understood. The need to secure the Clean Coasts Fund grant before the deadline created urgency, with calls to manage grid upgrade costs carefully.

Overall, the simulation indicates that while initial resistance centered on service reductions and fare hikes was significant, comprehensive stakeholder engagement and highlighting clear benefits can shift community opinion toward strong support for sustainable ferry electrification. Crucially, balancing service reliability—especially during winter months—and manageable fare increases appears essential to maintain community accessibility and economic resilience alongside achieving climate goals. Policymakers face the challenge of negotiating these trade-offs within budget caps and infrastructure constraints to deliver a solution that gains broad-based consent.

sections.title: Business and Economic Implications
sections.body:
The scenario simulation of stakeholder responses on Larkholm Island to the proposal of replacing the aging diesel ferry MV Gannet with a battery-electric vessel reveals a notable evolution of opinion from mixed initial reactions to overwhelming support by the final rounds. The Residents' Association accordingly requested council guarantees to maintain six winter sailings and cap fare increases at 5%, pledging not to oppose an electric ferry that met these criteria (S5).

Over six rounds on two platforms, discourse data showed mean opinion rising from a low starting point (approx. 0.15) to above 0.9 final support, with opposition dropping from 50-33% to zero and polarization declining markedly (timeline). Engagement across rounds included stakeholders articulating concerns but gradually converging on the electric ferry’s net benefits when environmental gains, fuel savings, and grant subsidy details were emphasized (M-plaza-2-agent-4, M-plaza-5-agent-4).

Council members and other moderate voices stressed the political and social necessity of maintaining at least six winter sailings and limiting fare increases to around 5%, despite financial and technical constraints, including a subsidy ceiling of $1.8 million and needed grid upgrades that delay ferry commission by 14–18 months (I1, I2, S1, S7). In summary, Larkholm stakeholders fundamentally support replacing the diesel ferry with a battery-electric vessel due to its strong environmental advantages and operational cost savings, especially with partial grant funding. The simulation underscores the critical importance of transparent community engagement, fiscal planning, and phased infrastructure upgrades to ensure the change strengthens Larkholm’s sustainability without undermining year-round accessibility and economic viability.

The environmental and economic advantages, bolstered by the Clean Coasts Fund grant, strongly support electrification. Nonetheless, maintaining at least six winter sailings and moderating fare increases are key conditions to preserve community access, sustain local economies dependent on year-round connectivity, and balance social and political considerations. initialPosts.text: The Council briefing note highlights rising maintenance costs and the end of the current ferry contract in 2028. They face a choice between a diesel refit costing $3.1M extending service 8 years or a $14.2M battery-electric replacement. The Clean Coasts Fund would pay 40% of the electric vessel if committed before Sept 30. There is political resistance to cutting winter service, but subsidy increase is capped at $1.8M. This frames the budget tension and timeline constraints.

The ferry company proposes a battery-electric ferry with a 12% fare increase and a reduced winter timetable of 4 daily return sailings (down from 6) from November to March, citing battery limitations in heavy weather and long grid upgrades. They warn missing the grant deadline risks losing the electric option. They also note fuel cost savings and emissions reductions of about 90%.

According to a residents' survey, 68% prioritize year-round reliability over emissions cuts, with 71% against reduced winter service and 64% opposing fare rises of 12%. However, 52% would support the electric ferry if 6 winter sailings daily are preserved. The community is concerned about winter dependencies like health trips and work commutes. The Residents' Association wants at least 6 winter sailings and max 5% fare increase to support the electric ferry.

Scenario assumptions set that the Council will commit before the grant deadline, allowing 40% Clean Coasts Fund support; fares will rise 12% and winter sailings drop to 4 daily; charging upgrades take about 16 months with diesel vessel running meanwhile; subsidy cap remains $1.8M; all stakeholders learn via public notice board and smaller community forums.

memories.text: The Council briefing note highlights rising maintenance costs and the end of the current ferry contract in 2028. They face a choice between a diesel refit costing $3.1M extending service 8 years or a $14.2M battery-electric replacement. The Clean Coasts Fund would pay 40% of the electric vessel if committed before Sept 30. There is political resistance to cutting winter service, but subsidy increase is capped at $1.8M. This frames the budget tension and timeline constraints.

According to a residents' survey, 68% prioritize year-round reliability over emissions cuts, with 71% against reduced winter service and 64% opposing fare rises of 12%. However, 52% would support the electric ferry if 6 winter sailings daily are preserved. The community is concerned about winter dependencies like health trips and work commutes. The Residents' Association wants at least 6 winter sailings and max 5% fare increase to support the electric ferry.

Scenario assumptions set that the Council will commit before the grant deadline, allowing 40% Clean Coasts Fund support; fares will rise 12% and winter sailings drop to 4 daily; charging upgrades take about 16 months with diesel vessel running meanwhile; subsidy cap remains $1.8M; all stakeholders learn via public notice board and smaller community forums.

The ferry company proposes a battery-electric ferry with a 12% fare increase and a reduced winter timetable of 4 daily return sailings (down from 6) from November to March, citing battery limitations in heavy weather and long grid upgrades. They warn missing the grant deadline risks losing the electric option. They also note fuel cost savings and emissions reductions of about 90%.

According to a residents' survey, 68% prioritize year-round reliability over emissions cuts, with 71% against reduced winter service and 64% opposing fare rises of 12%. However, 52% would support the electric ferry if 6 winter sailings daily are preserved. The community is concerned about winter dependencies like health trips and work commutes. The Residents' Association wants at least 6 winter sailings and max 5% fare increase to support the electric ferry.

While the shift to a battery-electric ferry aligns with sustainability aims and funding opportunity, cutting winter sailings to 4 daily risks violating core community priorities and political stability. We must advocate holding winter service at 6 sailings and explore further cost efficiencies or phased fare increases within the $1.8M subsidy cap.
memories.rationale: Council notes maintenance and contract timeline; community strongly opposes winter service cuts, risking political fallout if ignored.

The fictional scenario on Larkholm Island reveals evolving community and stakeholder perspectives regarding the proposed replacement of the island's aging diesel ferry MV Gannet with a battery-electric vessel. Initially, opinions were notably mixed and divided. Early rounds on both the Info Plaza and Topic Community platforms showed moderate mean support (around 0.28 to 0.43) with significant polarization (above 0.5), reflecting concerns over two main factors: the reduction of winter sailings from six to four daily return crossings and a proposed 12% fare increase. Many residents and stakeholders feared that fewer winter sailings could undermine essential transport access in off-peak months, impacting health appointments, work commutes, and local economic activity. The fare increase raised worries about deterring visitors, particularly in the vital summer season, potentially harming the island's visitor economy.

Over the course of six discussion rounds, however, opinions converged strongly in favor of the electric ferry. By the final round, mean opinion scores rose sharply to approximately 0.92, with unanimous support and zero opposition, while polarization decreased substantially (to below 0.15), indicating consensus formation. This shift was driven largely by emphasis on the substantial environmental benefits of the electric ferry—roughly a 90% cut in emissions—and economic savings of about $0.9 million annually in fuel costs. The Clean Coasts Fund's 40% capital grant also factored prominently, making the electric vessel financially feasible within existing subsidy constraints.

Stakeholders such as the fictional Green Tide Alliance and Harbour Business Council publicly supported the electric ferry, recognizing its alignment with Larkholm's green branding and sustainability commitments. They did, however, call for mitigating the reduced winter service by reallocating summer fare revenues and urged the Council to keep fare increases to a more moderate level to protect visitor numbers. Residents surveyed by the Larkholm Residents' Association expressed conditional support: 52% favored the electric ferry if winter sailings remained at six and fare rises were capped at 5%. Concerns about impacts on essential travel and economic vitality persisted, especially from councillors representing harbour ward, who stated political opposition to winter service cuts.

Fictional memory posts and interviews highlight these dialectics. Early community posts show caution or opposition due to fare and timetable cuts, emphasizing the importance of year-round reliability for medical appointments, work, and tourism. Later interactions underscore growing acceptance as environmental and cost savings were more clearly communicated and understood. The need to secure the Clean Coasts Fund grant before the deadline created urgency, with calls to manage grid upgrade costs carefully.

Overall, the simulation indicates that while initial resistance centered on service reductions and fare hikes was significant, comprehensive stakeholder engagement and highlighting clear benefits can shift community opinion toward strong support for sustainable ferry electrification. Crucially, balancing service reliability—especially during winter months—and manageable fare increases appears essential to maintain community accessibility and economic resilience alongside achieving climate goals. Policymakers face the challenge of negotiating these trade-offs within budget caps and infrastructure constraints to deliver a solution that gains broad-based consent.

Over six rounds of discussions spanning 180 minutes on two separate platforms, stakeholder discourse became progressively more favorable. This shift coincided with reinforced arguments emphasizing the environmental advantages, chiefly an approximately 90% reduction in operating emissions and projected annual fuel savings nearing $0.9 million. The simulated scenario on Larkholm island assessed stakeholder responses to replacing the island's aging diesel ferry, the MV Gannet, with a new battery-electric vessel that would achieve roughly a 90% reduction in fuel use and emissions, and save about $0.9 million annually in fuel costs. This electric vessel would be partially funded by a 40% Clean Coasts Fund grant contingent on early commitment. However, the proposal also includes reducing the winter ferry timetable from six to four daily return sailings and increasing fares by 12%, presenting significant challenges for community acceptance.

Initial stakeholder opinions were mixed and polarized, reflecting concerns about reduced winter service disrupting essential travel for residents and fare increases potentially harming the local visitor economy. The winter timetable cut was particularly contentious because island residents rely heavily on year-round ferry access for health appointments, work commutes, and other critical travel. Surveys indicated that 71% of islander respondents opposed reduced winter sailings, and 64% opposed a 12% fare increase. Yet, 52% indicated conditional support for an electric ferry if at least six winter sailings were maintained.

By the final rounds, mean opinion rose to over 92%, with unanimous support and zero opposition, and polarization markedly decreased. This change was driven in part by emphasis on environmental benefits, including substantial emission cuts and fuel savings, alongside the clear financial incentive of the Clean Coasts Fund grant covering 40% of costs. Stakeholders from environmental groups, such as the Green Tide Alliance, strongly advocated for accepting the grant and focusing on climate goals even if winter services were reduced, suggesting that summer fare revenue could subsidize winter trips.

However, elected representatives and business stakeholders voiced the necessity of preserving sufficient winter sailings and limiting fare increases to socially and politically acceptable levels. The Larkholm Residents' Association argued for guaranteeing at least six daily winter ferries and capping fare rises at 5%, warning that cuts below this level could jeopardize essential travel for health and work and erode community support. Similarly, the Harbour Business Council supported the electric ferry due to its green branding and cost-saving potential but cautioned that higher fares and reduced winter service risked deterring visitors critical to the summer economy.

In interviews with simulated council members and ferry company leadership, the balance between operational and technical constraints—such as the need for 14-18 months of charging infrastructure upgrades before the electric vessel's commissioning—and community needs received attention. The ferry company noted that reduced winter sailings help protect battery health and accommodate charging schedules but acknowledged customer acceptance uncertainties. Council members emphasized the political difficulty of endorsing winter service reductions amid essential resident dependency and recommended controlled fare increases under 5% to maintain affordability and accessibility.

In summary, the scenario points to a growing consensus on the net benefits of transitioning to the battery-electric ferry on Larkholm if mitigations are implemented. The environmental and economic advantages, bolstered by the Clean Coasts Fund grant, strongly support electrification. Nonetheless, maintaining at least six winter sailings and moderating fare increases are key conditions to preserve community access, sustain local economies dependent on year-round connectivity, and balance social and political considerations. The simulation reveals the critical interplay between advancing sustainability goals and ensuring reliable, affordable transport to safeguard the island's social fabric and economic vitality in council deliberations.

interviews.answer: Replacing the island ferry MV Gannet with a battery-electric vessel offers significant environmental and economic benefits, including a roughly 90% reduction in fuel use and emissions, plus annual fuel cost savings around $0.9 million. This aligns well with Larkholm's sustainability goals and leverages a 40% Clean Coasts Fund grant if committed before the deadline, easing upfront investment burdens. However, the proposed accompanying reduction in the winter timetable from six to four daily return sailings presents major challenges. Constituents, especially those represented by harbour ward council members like myself (Cllr Norton), strongly rely on at least six winter sailings for essential travel, viewing any cut as politically and socially unacceptable. interviews.answer:
As CEO of Larkholm Ferry Company, I perceive replacing the island ferry with a battery-electric vessel as a positive step toward operational efficiency, significant long-term cost savings (around $0.9 million annually), and a major reduction in emissions (about 90%). This modernization aligns with sustainability goals and enhances the island's green image. However, I anticipate challenges related to the technical feasibility and reliability of the new electric ferry, particularly regarding the need for substantial grid upgrades at both terminals, which will take approximately 14 to 18 months. During this interim, continuing the current diesel ferry service is essential to maintain reliable transport.

Reducing the winter timetable from six to four daily return sailings helps protect the battery and accommodate charging demands but may raise community concerns, especially as some stakeholders emphasize maintaining at least six winter sailings to support essential year-round connectivity. Customer acceptance of reduced winter service and a planned fare increase (capped at about 10-12%) remains uncertain, which poses risks to passenger satisfaction and usage levels.

Balancing these operational constraints with community needs requires transparent engagement, maintaining minimum winter service levels as much as possible, and carefully managing pricing to avoid deterring visitors and residents. Overall, the benefits include substantial emissions cuts, cost savings, and modernization of the service, while the challenges revolve around managing the transition period reliability, technical infrastructure readiness, and community acceptance of service reductions and fare changes.
